cues.text: Begin with the young anther in transverse section.
A labels one of four microsporangia in the typical bilobed model.
Each lobe contains two of these sacs.
B points to the connective joining the lobes, and C to its selected vascular
bundle.
The small dots represent selected sporogenous cells at this stage, not a count
of mature pollen grains.
Do not confuse a whole anther lobe with one microsporangium.
Development changes the appearance of the sacs and walls, so a mature dehisced
anther need not look exactly like this young section.
Read the stage and view before applying a memorised count.
Keep the anther board and add developmental meaning.
Sporogenous cells can become microspore mother cells.
A diploid mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce a tetrad of haploid
microspores.
Each microspore can develop into a pollen grain, the male gametophyte.
A microspore is therefore not already a male gamete.
The three small dots selected within each sac do not imply that only three
microspores form or that a tetrad has three members.
Their purpose is to locate the tissue region.
Distinguish the organ, the sporangium, the mother cell, the spore and the
later
gametophyte as separate levels.
The enlarged microsporangium board separates four wall regions.
From outside inward, A is epidermis, B endothecium, C the middle layer zone
and D tapetum.
E marks the central sporogenous tissue.
Trace the leader endpoints and follow the order rather than counting every
outline as another tissue.
A zone can contain more than one cell layer, and the simplified boundaries are
not an exact cell inventory.
Tapetum is the innermost wall layer next to the developing reproductive cells.
The sporogenous tissue at the centre is not a fifth wall layer.
This young stage board does not claim that all wall regions persist unchanged
at maturity.
Connect position with function.
The tapetum supplies support and nutrition to developing microspores and
contributes materials involved in pollen development.
The endothecium participates in the mechanical changes associated with anther
dehiscence.
Do not swap these roles simply because both are wall tissues.
The wall layers belong to the sporophyte; they are not themselves the haploid
pollen generation.
Tapetal cells may have more than one nucleus and can show varied nuclear
states.
Nuclear number alone does not determine ploidy.
The drawing does not measure chromosome number or show the later pattern of
wall breakdown, so use the stated developmental context rather than inventing
details from the outlines.
Move to the selected ovule section.
A marks the micropylar opening left by the integuments.
B points to an integument zone, the protective covering around internal
tissues.
F labels the funicle, the stalk attaching the ovule, and H its junction with
the ovule, called the hilum.
The micropyle is not the hilum, and an integument is not the embryo sac.
The two open covering outlines are schematic and do not establish the exact
number of cell layers.
Ovule orientation varies among plants; this selected drawing is designed for
local structure labels rather than a complete species or orientation
diagnosis.
C identifies nucellus, the tissue surrounding the embryo sac labelled D.
E marks the chalazal region opposite the micropyle.
The embryo sac is the female gametophyte, while nucellus and integuments are
maternal sporophytic tissues.
Do not assign the same ploidy to all structures merely because they share one
ovule.
In the usual monosporic pathway, meiosis of a megaspore mother cell produces
megaspores, one of which develops into the embryo sac.
After normal seed formation, the ovule becomes a seed and integuments
contribute to its coat.
The ovary usually develops into the fruit.
An ovule is not a miniature ovary.
The final board enlarges a typical embryo sac.
Its chalazal end is above and micropylar end below.
A marks three antipodal cells.
C points to the egg, with the two synergids labelled D beside it.
Egg plus two synergids form the egg apparatus at the micropylar end.
Short bars at the micropylar tips of the synergids represent the filiform
apparatus, which helps guide the pollen tube.
The larger middle region is one central cell.
These are selected shapes, not an exact scale model of every flowering plant.
Use end orientation before naming a group of three cells; antipodals and egg
apparatus are not interchangeable.
B identifies two polar nuclei within one large central cell.
Count the three antipodals, two synergids, one egg and one central cell: seven
cells.
At the illustrated stage before polar nuclear fusion, the six smaller cells
contain six nuclei, and the central cell contains two, giving eight nuclei.
The two polar nuclei are not two extra cells.
They may fuse to form a secondary nucleus, so a later stage need not display
two separate central nuclei.
During normal double fertilisation, one male gamete fuses with the egg and the
other with the central cell nuclear complement.
This board depicts the typical pre fertilisation model, not a fertilised
embryo
or every embryo sac type.
